title: How to Do Nothing: Resisting the Attention Economy
author: Jenny Odell
target_audience: Adults interested in digital wellness and mindfulness
Readers concerned about technology’s influence on society
Critics of social media and the attention economy
Individuals seeking alternative approaches to productivity and time management
Academics and students in media studies, philosophy, and contemporary culture
core_themes: Resisting the commodification of attention in the digital age
The importance of presence, observation, and local community
Reclaiming autonomy from social media and technology platforms
primary_purpose: To challenge readers to reconsider what it means to be productive, and to offer philosophical, historical, and personal reflections on how to resist the pervasive demands of the attention economy in order to cultivate deeper forms of presence, connection, and meaning.

structure_format.narrative_style: Reflective, essayistic, and philosophical with elements of memoir
structure_format.organization: Arranged in thematically focused chapters blending personal narrative, cultural history, philosophy, and case studies
features: Interweaving of autobiographical experience with analysis
Citations from writers, philosophers, and activists
Emphasis on nature, art, and community

key_concepts_lessons: The attention economy exploits human psychology for profit, fragmenting focus and autonomy.
Refusing to participate in constant online activity is a form of resistance and reclamation.
True ‘doing nothing’ involves becoming attentively present to the world, not mere passivity.
Community engagement and ecological awareness are antidotes to isolation and consumer culture.
Slowness, idleness, and observation are necessary for creative thought and genuine connection.
Reclaiming attention isn’t about permanent disconnection, but about choosing how and where to engage meaningfully.
notable_features: Critique of Silicon Valley’s technology and work culture (author’s personal proximity to the Bay Area)
Integrates art, ecology, and political activism in its critique
Rejects simplistic self-improvement rhetoric for a broader social and ethical perspective
Rich in cultural and historical references
cultural_historical_context: Published in an era of unprecedented social media influence, rise of digital distraction, polarization, and tech industry growth, particularly in the San Francisco Bay Area. The book emerged alongside rising concerns over mental health, burnout, and loss of civic engagement tied to the attention economy.
reception_impact: Widely acclaimed for its originality and depth, often cited in discussions of digital minimalism and tech criticism
Recognized as a foundational text of the ‘digital wellness’ and tech resistance movements
Featured on multiple ‘Best Books’ lists and praised for combining personal reflection with cultural critique
Critics note its lack of concrete solutions but celebrate its probing questions and literary style
comparable_titles: The Art of Noticing by Rob Walker
